title: Continuity and differentiability of Thomae’s function
notes: Exercise 1 asks for the continuity and differentiability of \(f(p/q)=1/q\) for reduced fractions and \(f(x)=0\) for irrational \(x\).
statement: On \(\mathbb R\), with \(q>0\) and \(\gcd(p,q)=1\), this function is continuous exactly at the irrational points and differentiable nowhere. At an irrational point, any derivative would be zero along irrational increments, whereas the convergents \(p_k/q_k\) satisfy \(|x-p_k/q_k|<q_k^{-2}\), so the absolute difference quotients exceed \(q_k\).
reconstruction: The domain, reduced denominators, and the short differentiability proof are explicit completion of the exercise.
fate: This is the classical Thomae example. \citet[pp.353--354]{varona2009differentiability} reproduces the exact function and proof; the 2009 article is a later exposition and extension, not the origin of this elementary result.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Differentiability of powers of Thomae’s function
notes: The same exercise asks what changes when \(1/q\) is replaced by \(1/q^\alpha\).
statement: For real \(\alpha\), let \(f_\alpha(p/q)=q^{-\alpha}\), \(f_\alpha(x)=0\) at irrationals. If \(\alpha\le0\), it is nowhere continuous; if \(\alpha>0\), continuity holds exactly at irrationals. It is nowhere differentiable for \(\alpha\le2\). For \(\alpha>2\) and irrational \(x=[a_0;a_1,\ldots]\) with convergent denominators \(q_k\), differentiability is equivalent to \(q_{k+1}/q_k^{\alpha-1}\to0\), and then \(f_\alpha^{\prime}(x)=0\). Equivalently, \(q^\alpha|x-p/q|\to\infty\) along all reduced rationals tending to \(x\).
reconstruction: The exact continued-fraction criterion is our explicit reformulation of the difference quotient. Necessity uses \((q_k(q_k+q_{k+1}))^{-1}<|x-p_k/q_k|<(q_kq_{k+1})^{-1}\); sufficiency also uses that a nonconvergent approximation has error at least \(1/(2q^2)\). Statements using only the irrationality exponent require care at equality.
fate: The family had already been studied by Nymann in 1969, as documented in \citet[introduction, \S\S1--3, reference 7]{varona2009differentiability}; that article gives further exact differentiability and measure statements. Thus the exercise is not classified as an unresolved 1980 conjecture. No assertion that the present denominator formulation first appeared in 1969 is made.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: A double continuous limit for the Dirichlet function
notes: Exercise 2 gives \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\lim_{m\to\infty}\cos^{2m}(2\pi n!x)\).
statement: For every real \(x\), this iterated limit equals \(\mathbf1_{\mathbb Q}(x)\). For fixed \(n\), the inner limit is one exactly when \(2n!x\in\mathbb Z\), and zero otherwise. Every rational satisfies the condition for all sufficiently large \(n\), whereas an irrational never does.
reconstruction: The order of limits is essential and is retained. This elementary calculation proves the formula without interchanging limits.
fate: This is the classical distinction between first and second Baire class. The underlying classification was established before 1900; \citet[p.173]{baire1900nouvelle} states the continuous-limit criterion. The displayed factorial formula is checked directly here, not attributed to that article.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Can the Dirichlet function be a pointwise limit of continuous functions?
notes: Exercise 3 asks whether a single sequence of continuous functions can tend pointwise to the Dirichlet function.
statement: No sequence \(g_j\in C(\mathbb R)\) converges at every real point to \(\mathbf1_{\mathbb Q}\). A real-valued Baire-class-one function has a dense \(G_\delta\) set of continuity points on every nonempty closed interval, while \(\mathbf1_{\mathbb Q}\) is nowhere continuous.
reconstruction: Pointwise convergence at every point is the required meaning; convergence almost everywhere would give a different, trivial answer.
fate: The negative answer is an immediate classical consequence of Baire's criterion; see \citet[p.173, opening theorem and reference to the 1899 thesis]{baire1900nouvelle}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Fourier integrals with quadratic, quartic, and sextic decay
notes: Exercise 4 asks for approximate values of \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\cos(1000x)\,dx\), and the analogues with \(x^4\) and \(x^6\).
statement: Write \(I_p(\lambda)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-x^p}\cos(\lambda x)\,dx\). Then \(I_2(1000)=\sqrt\pi e^{-250000}\). For \(p=4,6\), put \(r=(\lambda/p)^{1/(p-1)}\), \(\theta=\pi/(2(p-1))\), \(A=(p-1)r^p\). As \(\lambda\to+\infty\), the two dominant conjugate saddle contributions give \[I_p(\lambda)=2\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{p(p-1)}}r^{-(p-2)/2}e^{-A\sin\theta}\left\{\cos\!\left(A\cos\theta-\frac{p-2}{2}\theta\right)+O(A^{-1})\right\}.\] The remainder is absolute relative to the displayed envelope, not relative to the cosine, which can vanish.
reconstruction: The parameter \(\lambda\), saddle computation, and error convention are supplied; the notebook asks only for approximations. Saddles solve \(pz^{p-1}=i\lambda\). The quartic and sextic formulas are explicit applications of the classical method, not a claimed new asymptotic theorem.
fate: Gaussian Fourier transformation and steepest descent predate the seminar. The simple-saddle expansion and branch convention are checked in \citet[\S2.4(iv), equations 2.4.15--16]{nist2026dlmf}; its cited pre-1980 sources include Olver and Bleistein--Handelsman. The displayed specialization is our calculation.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Pullback of a left D-module
notes: For \(f:X\to Y\), the notes put \(f^*M=\mathcal O_X\otimes_{f^{-1}\mathcal O_Y}f^{-1}M\) and differentiate both factors through \(df\).
statement: Let \(X,Y\) be smooth varieties over a characteristic-zero field and \(M\) a left \(\mathcal D_Y\)-module quasicoherent over \(\mathcal O_Y\). If \(df(v)=\sum_i a_i\otimes w_i\), the pullback left action is \(v(b\otimes m)=v(b)\otimes m+\sum_i ba_i\otimes w_i m\). The resulting module is independent of the local expression for \(df(v)\).
reconstruction: Smoothness, characteristic zero, and the inverse-image sheaves are written explicitly. This is the ordinary tensor pullback; it need not preserve coherent \(\mathcal D\)-modules.
fate: This is the standard inverse-image construction of algebraic \(\mathcal D\)-module theory. The exact bimodule and action are read in \citet[\S7 and \S13]{gourevitch2025dmodules}; the contemporary framework is already represented by \citet[\S1]{bernstein1971modules}. The 2025 course is used as a precise later exposition, not a priority date.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Pullback of connections and of the structure sheaf
notes: The pullback agrees with the usual pullback of a bundle with flat connection, and \(f^*\mathcal O_Y=\mathcal O_X\).
statement: For a finite-rank algebraic vector bundle \((E,\nabla)\) with integrable connection on smooth \(Y\), the displayed module action gives the integrable pullback connection on \(f^*E\); the trivial connection on \(\mathcal O_Y\) pulls back to the trivial connection on \(\mathcal O_X\).
fate: The compatibility is part of the classical connection--\(\mathcal D\)-module correspondence; compare \citet[Lemma 9.11 and inverse-image construction]{gourevitch2025dmodules}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Ordinary pullback can destroy D-module coherence
notes: For a point inclusion \(i:x\hookrightarrow Y\), the fibre of the free module \(\mathcal D_Y\) is the infinite-dimensional space of constant-coefficient differential operators.
statement: If \(\dim Y=d>0\), then \(i^*\mathcal D_Y\simeq k[\partial_1,\ldots,\partial_d]\) as a module over \(\mathcal D_{\{x\}}=k\). Thus a coherent \(\mathcal D_Y\)-module can have an ordinary inverse image that is not coherent over \(k\).
reconstruction: The polynomial description uses local smooth coordinates and the positive-dimensional assumption.
fate: The example follows directly from the Weyl-algebra normal form; see \citet[\S1.2 and inverse images]{gourevitch2025dmodules}. It is a classical warning about inverse images, not a later counterexample to holonomic stability.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The ordinary fibre of a delta module vanishes
notes: The notes assert \(i^*\delta_x=0\), justifying it with the written identity \(\delta(y)=y\delta^{\prime}(y)\).
statement: For the left delta module at the origin of \(\mathbb A^d\), \(\delta_0\simeq k[\partial_1,\ldots,\partial_d]\), one has \(x_i\partial^\alpha\delta_0=-\alpha_i\partial^{\alpha-e_i}\delta_0\). Consequently each coordinate acts surjectively and \(k\otimes_{\mathcal O_{\mathbb A^d}}\delta_0=0\). The derived fibre is nonzero; in the unshifted tensor convention its only cohomology is \(k\) in degree \(-d\).
reconstruction: The sign is repaired: \(y\delta^{\prime}=-\delta\). Derived and ordinary pullbacks are distinguished; the Koszul-complex calculation supplies the derived degree.
fate: The delta-module and closed-embedding calculations are classical; see \citet[Example 9.5 and Theorem 9.1]{gourevitch2025dmodules}. The sign follows from differentiating \(y\delta=0\).
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The transfer bimodule and ordinary right direct image
notes: The notebook defines \(\mathcal D_{X\to Y}=f^*\mathcal D_Y\) and \(f_*M=f_\bullet(M\otimes_{\mathcal D_X}\mathcal D_{X\to Y})\) for right modules.
statement: For a morphism of smooth varieties, \(\mathcal D_{X\to Y}=\mathcal O_X\otimes_{f^{-1}\mathcal O_Y}f^{-1}\mathcal D_Y\) is a \((\mathcal D_X,f^{-1}\mathcal D_Y)\)-bimodule. Its underived direct image sends a right module \(M\) to \(f_\bullet(M\otimes_{\mathcal D_X}\mathcal D_{X\to Y})\).
reconstruction: The subscript \(\bullet\) is reserved for ordinary sheaf direct image, avoiding confusion with the differential-module direct image.
fate: This transfer-module construction is classical and appears with the derived version in \citet[\S13]{gourevitch2025dmodules}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Closed-embedding direct images and normal delta derivatives
notes: Pushing a scalar at a point gives a delta module; a closed embedding of a subvariety adds delta functions and derivatives in transverse directions.
statement: If \(i:X\hookrightarrow Y\) is a closed embedding of smooth varieties, the right direct image is exact and locally adjoins freely the normal derivatives to a right \(\mathcal D_X\)-module. At a coordinate origin it sends \(k\) to \(\mathcal D_Y/\sum_j y_j\mathcal D_Y\) as a right module.
reconstruction: The closed and smooth hypotheses are essential. The quotient is a right-module quotient by the right ideal generated by multiplication by the coordinates, not its left-module analogue.
fate: The exact identification is the closed-embedding calculation underlying Kashiwara's equivalence; \citet[Theorem 9.1, Example 9.5]{gourevitch2025dmodules} gives the read modern formulation.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Canonical right module and conversion from left modules
notes: Top-degree forms, and top-degree forms valued in a flat bundle, are presented as natural right modules.
statement: For smooth \(X\), \(\omega_X=\Omega_X^{\dim X}\) has the right action \(\eta\cdot v=-\mathcal L_v\eta\). Tensoring a left module \(E\) with \(\omega_X\) gives a right module, with \((\eta\otimes e)\cdot v=(\eta\cdot v)\otimes e-\eta\otimes ve\). This is an equivalence between left and right \(\mathcal D_X\)-modules.
reconstruction: The signs and the full equivalence are supplied to make the note about volume forms precise.
fate: The standard left/right conversion is read in \citet[Exercise 7.16]{gourevitch2025dmodules}; it belongs to the established theory used in the talk.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Derived pullback and derived integration
notes: The notes replace pullback by \(Lf^*\) and define \(\int M=Rf_\bullet(M\otimes^L_{\mathcal D_X}\mathcal D_{X\to Y})\), with its cohomology objects \(\int^iM\).
statement: For bounded complexes of quasicoherent right \(\mathcal D_X\)-modules, define \(f_+M=Rf_\bullet(M\otimes^L_{\mathcal D_X}\mathcal D_{X\to Y})\). For left modules, the unshifted inverse image is \(\mathcal D_{X\to Y}\otimes^L_{f^{-1}\mathcal D_Y}f^{-1}N\). These derived functors retain the higher Tor and sheaf-cohomology terms lost by ordinary operations.
reconstruction: A bounded setting and the distinction from dimension-shifted extraordinary inverse image are stated explicitly.
fate: These are established derived operations; see \citet[\S13]{gourevitch2025dmodules} and the derived-functor formalism in \citet[\S10.5]{weibel1994homological}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Integration of the canonical module computes shifted de Rham cohomology
notes: For smooth complex \(X\), the final formula is \(\int^i\omega_X=H^{\dim X+i}(X,\mathbb C)\).
statement: If \(X\) is a smooth complex algebraic variety of dimension \(d\), and \(p:X\to\mathrm{pt}\), then \(p_+\omega_X\simeq R\Gamma(X,\Omega_X^\bullet)[d]\). Hence \(H^i(p_+\omega_X)\simeq H^{i+d}(X^{\mathrm{an}},\mathbb C)\) by algebraic de Rham comparison. This is ordinary cohomology, not cohomology with compact support.
reconstruction: The algebraic/analytic comparison and the cohomological shift convention are made explicit. Properness is unnecessary for this ordinary algebraic de Rham comparison.
fate: The de Rham description of direct image is classical; see \citet[\S13, de Rham direct image]{gourevitch2025dmodules}. The notebook states an already established comparison, rather than a new 1980 theorem.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Isomorphic cohomology need not lift to a chain map
notes: Exercise 1 says that an isomorphism of the cohomology of two complexes need not extend to a chain map inducing it.
statement: In complexes of abelian groups, let \(A=(\mathbb Z/2)[0]\), and let \(B\) be \(\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb Z\) in degrees \(-1,0\). Both have only \(H^0\simeq\mathbb Z/2\). Every chain map \(A\to B\) is zero because \(\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb Z/2,\mathbb Z)=0\); hence none induces the prescribed identity on \(H^0\). They are nevertheless isomorphic in the derived category through the quasi-isomorphism \(B\to A\).
reconstruction: The explicit example and the direction of the attempted map are supplied. Over a field, complexes split and this particular obstruction disappears; the ambient abelian category cannot be omitted.
fate: This is established homological algebra, explained by localization at quasi-isomorphisms; see \citet[\S\S10.1--10.3]{weibel1994homological}. It continues earlier seminar discussions of the derived-category universal property, especially 1971-266.3.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: An unspecified derived equivalence between a sphere and its dual
notes: The notes write sheaf categories \(C,C_1\) on \(S^n,S^{*n}\), an \(O(n)\)-action, \(C_1\not\simeq C\) because the action differs, and \(D(S)\sim D(S^*)\).
statement: An exact equivalence cannot be specified from the record: the definition of the dual sphere, the action on each category, the coefficients and boundedness or constructibility restrictions, and the transforming kernel are absent. With the standard Euclidean duality and orthogonal action, the spheres are already equivariantly isomorphic, so their ordinary sheaf categories are equivalent; that literal reading does not produce the claimed distinction.
reconstruction: No Radon-transform equivalence is substituted for the missing assertion. Such a reconstruction would require extra geometry not fixed by the manuscript.
fate: Searches for S. I. Gelfand, dual spheres, equivariant sheaves, and derived/Radon transformations did not establish an exact publication match. \citet[Chapter 10]{weibel1994homological} supplies only the general derived-category language, not this claimed equivalence.
present_status: As of November 2026, the exact assertion and its fate remain unidentifiable from the surviving formulation; this is a source ambiguity, not a well-posed open problem.

title: Whitehead product from the boundary of a product of cubes
notes: The notes write \(\pi_n(X)\times\pi_m(X)\to\pi_{n+m}(X)\) and decompose \(\partial(I^n\times I^m)\).
statement: For a pointed space and \(n,m\ge2\), the Whitehead product is \([\ ,\ ]:\pi_n(X)\times\pi_m(X)\to\pi_{n+m-1}(X)\). Representatives on \(I^n/\partial I^n\) and \(I^m/\partial I^m\) define the map on the two pieces of the boundary of \(I^n\times I^m\), agreeing at the basepoint on their intersection.
reconstruction: The target is corrected by one degree; the boundary has dimension \(n+m-1\). Low-dimensional nonabelian variants are not needed for the next graded statement.
fate: This is Whitehead's classical construction; the attaching-map formulation is read in \citet[\S4.2, p.381]{hatcher2002algebraic}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Shifted graded Jacobi identity for Whitehead products
notes: The note compares the product to a Lie bracket and says that the Jacobi identity holds, with a “super” sign convention.
statement: After the usual sign adjustment identifying Whitehead products with Samelson products in \(\Omega X\), the graded group \(L_d=\pi_{d+1}(X)\), \(d\ge1\), satisfies \([a,b]=-(-1)^{|a||b|}[b,a]\) and \((-1)^{|a||c|}[a,[b,c]]+(-1)^{|b||a|}[b,[c,a]]+(-1)^{|c||b|}[c,[a,b]]=0\). Over \(\mathbb Z\), torsion can prevent the alternating axiom \([a,a]=0\) in even degree; after tensoring with \(\mathbb Q\), this is a graded Lie algebra in the usual sense.
reconstruction: The degree shift and the integral torsion caveat are supplied. The notebook's analogy should not be read as an unrestricted ordinary Lie algebra on unshifted homotopy groups.
fate: The identity predates the talk by decades. \citet[p.180, publisher extract]{hilton1961jacobi} explicitly describes the already-known identity; the 1961 print date is distinct from the 2008 digital posting. Only the extract, not the full three-page proof, was read.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: An ambiguous four-operator perturbation assertion
notes: The manuscript has \(A-A^{\prime}\) nuclear, \([B,A]=[B,A^{\prime}]=0\), \(B-B^{\prime}\) completely continuous, and concludes \(B|_{\mathcal H_{ac}(B)}\simeq B^{\prime}|_{\mathcal H_{ac}(B^{\prime})}\). It then proposes treating commuting families directly.
statement: The exact intended theorem is undetermined. A valid nearby statement is: for bounded self-adjoint \(A,A^{\prime},B,B^{\prime}\), if \(A-A^{\prime}\) is trace class, \([A,B]=[A^{\prime},B^{\prime}]=0\), and \(B-B^{\prime}\) is compact, the complete wave operators \(W_\pm(A^{\prime},A)\) intertwine \(B|_{\mathcal H_{ac}(A)}\) and \(B^{\prime}|_{\mathcal H_{ac}(A^{\prime})}\). They are unitary between those two spectral subspaces.
reconstruction: This repair changes both the second commutator and the operators defining the absolutely continuous subspaces; it is ours, not a corrected reading. Indeed \(e^{-itA}u\rightharpoonup0\) on \(\mathcal H_{ac}(A)\), so \((B^{\prime}-B)e^{-itA}u\to0\) in norm. Passing to the wave-operator limit proves the extra intertwining. The literal conditions, with \(A=A^{\prime}=0\), would impose no control beyond compact perturbation on \(B,B^{\prime}\), which is insufficient to preserve absolutely continuous spectrum.
fate: \citet[Theorem 1, pp.260--261]{kato1957trace} proves the required complete wave operators, already in 1957. The compact-perturbation counterexample follows from the classical Weyl--von Neumann theorem, whose exact statement is read in \citet[Theorem 1.1]{andomatsuzawa2014weyl}. Lomonosov's \citet[pp.54--55]{lomonosov1980intertwiner} is a bibliographically verified contemporary lead, received 11 December 1978; its full text was not retrieved and it is not claimed as a match. The commuting-family remark has no recoverable additional hypotheses.
present_status: As of November 2026, the repaired statement is a standard consequence of trace-class scattering theory, but the exact Lomonosov assertion and its publication fate remain unresolved at the source-identification level. No open mathematical problem is inferred.

title: Pulling solutions back and integrating solutions along fibres
notes: The transfer-module formulas are repeated with the explanation that pullback carries solutions to solutions and direct image supplies equations for integrals, including improper integrals.
statement: For a morphism of smooth characteristic-zero varieties, inverse-image modules encode the chain rule and derived direct-image modules encode relative de Rham classes. In an analytic realization, an integral of a differential form solving a \(\mathcal D_X\)-system gives a solution of the appropriate direct-image system when differentiation under the integral and integration by parts are valid, for example along a proper smoothly varying closed cycle or with controlled compact support.
reconstruction: The analytic convergence, boundary, and differentiation conditions are supplied; the bare module formula does not justify arbitrary improper integration.
fate: This is the established direct-image interpretation of differential equations and periods; see \citet[\S13, especially the de Rham and Gauss--Manin discussion]{gourevitch2025dmodules}. It repeats the construction of 1980-500.5 and develops its analytic meaning.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Derived direct images compose
notes: The underived operation is said not to satisfy composition; equation (7) states \(Rg_*Rf_*=R(g\circ f)_*\).
statement: For morphisms \(X\xrightarrow fY\xrightarrow gZ\) of smooth varieties in characteristic zero, the derived right-module direct images satisfy a natural isomorphism \(g_+f_+\simeq(gf)_+\) on the bounded quasicoherent derived categories where these operations are defined. The ordinary tensor-and-sheaf-direct-image construction can lose higher cohomology and does not in general have this property.
reconstruction: The notation \(f_+\) distinguishes this operation from the ordinary derived direct image of sheaves. The assertion concerns natural derived isomorphisms, not equality of chosen complexes.
fate: The exact composition theorem is read in \citet[Theorem 13.22]{gourevitch2025dmodules}. Its mechanism is associativity of derived tensor products and the derived projection formula, established before this expository lecture.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Projection of a plane and the degree minus one direct image
notes: For the projection of a plane to a line, the direct image of volume forms has zero degree-zero component and volume forms on the line in degree \(-1\).
statement: For the algebraic projection \(f:\mathbb A^2\to\mathbb A^1\) over a characteristic-zero field, \(f_+\omega_{\mathbb A^2}\simeq\omega_{\mathbb A^1}[1]\). Its only cohomology is \(H^{-1}=\omega_{\mathbb A^1}\). Relative de Rham cohomology of the affine-line fibre is concentrated in unshifted degree zero.
reconstruction: The notes' word “component” is read as a cohomology object, not a canonical zero/nonzero pattern for every representative complex. The affine algebraic setting fixes the cohomology convention.
fate: This elementary instance of the relative de Rham description is verified from \citet[\S13]{gourevitch2025dmodules}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The right-module Spencer complex and de Rham shift
notes: The complex \(\cdots\to M\otimes\Lambda^2T_X\to M\otimes T_X\to M\) computes direct image to a point. For volume forms, it is called the de Rham complex shifted to the left by a symbol transcribed as \(M\).
statement: For a right module \(M\) on smooth \(d\)-dimensional \(X\), the Spencer differential uses the right vector-field action and Lie brackets on \(M\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}\Lambda^jT_X\), placed in degree \(-j\). This complex computes \(M\otimes^L_{\mathcal D_X}\mathcal O_X\); applying \(R\Gamma\) computes \(p_+M\). For \(M=\omega_X\), contraction identifies it with \(\Omega_X^\bullet[d]\).
reconstruction: The shift is \(d=\dim X\), as confirmed by the following displayed formula \(R^ip_*\omega_X=H^{d+i}(X)\); the ambiguous handwritten symbol cannot serve as a shift index.
fate: The Spencer resolution and de Rham interpretation are standard; see \citet[\S13]{gourevitch2025dmodules}. This makes explicit the calculation already announced in 1980-500.9.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Relative de Rham cohomology and the Gauss–Manin action
notes: For a smooth morphism, the relative tangent complex is pushed forward and receives a \(\mathcal D_Y\)-action called the Gauss--Manin connection.
statement: If \(f:X\to Y\) is smooth between smooth varieties, the relative Spencer complex computes direct image after the canonical left/right conversion and the appropriate relative-dimension shift. For a smooth proper morphism and a finite-rank integrable connection on \(X\), its relative de Rham cohomology sheaves are locally free and carry integrable Gauss--Manin connections, compatible with the \(\mathcal D_Y\)-module direct image.
reconstruction: The canonical-bundle conversion is necessary for a right-module formula: locally \(\omega_X\simeq\omega_{X/Y}\otimes f^*\omega_Y\). Properness is added only for the stated finite-rank bundle conclusion; without it the direct image is still a derived \(\mathcal D\)-module and need not be a vector bundle.
fate: The exact smooth-proper connection statement and its qualifications are read in \citet[\S13, Gauss--Manin discussion]{gourevitch2025dmodules}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Closed-embedding exactness and Kashiwara equivalence
notes: For an “embedding”, both direct-image steps are said to be exact; volume forms become delta forms in normal directions.
statement: For a closed embedding \(i:X\hookrightarrow Y\) of smooth varieties, the transfer bimodule is flat for the required left \(\mathcal D_X\)-action, and \(i_+\) is exact on modules. It identifies \(\mathcal D_X\)-modules with \(\mathcal D_Y\)-modules supported on \(X\), with an inverse given by the appropriate degree of extraordinary restriction.
reconstruction: “Closed” must be supplied; an arbitrary open or locally closed embedding does not make ordinary sheaf direct image exact in the same fashion.
fate: This is Kashiwara's equivalence, read in \citet[Theorem 9.1]{gourevitch2025dmodules} and independently in \citet[\S8]{bernstein1982dmodules}. The later lecture notes are verification sources for an already established theorem.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Holonomicity tested by all derived point fibres
notes: A finitely generated module is called holonomic if the cohomology of \(Li_x^*M\) is finite-dimensional for every point. The free module is explicitly excluded.
statement: For a coherent \(\mathcal D_X\)-module on a smooth complex algebraic variety, holonomicity is equivalent to finite-dimensional cohomology of its derived inverse image at every closed point. Equivalently, its nonempty characteristic variety has dimension \(\dim X\). A nonzero locally free \(\mathcal D_X\)-module is not holonomic if \(\dim X>0\). Dimension shifts between \(i^*\) and \(i^!\) do not affect this finiteness test.
reconstruction: Coherence, the complex algebraic category, and derived rather than ordinary fibres are essential. For example, the ordinary fibre of a delta module vanishes, while its derived fibre does not.
fate: The exact converse as well as the forward implication are read in \citet[Proposition 16.6]{gourevitch2025dmodules}. The foundational dimension framework is in \citet[\S\S1--3]{bernstein1971modules}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Generic connections and gluing holonomic modules along strata
notes: The examples say that a holonomic module is a flat bundle away from exceptional points or curves, and ask whether all such modules are glued from transverse delta modules.
statement: A holonomic module has a finite algebraic stratification of its support such that the appropriate restrictions to smooth strata are finite-rank integrable connections. Its simple constituents are minimal extensions of irreducible connections on dense smooth locally closed strata; general holonomic modules are finite successive extensions of these. This does not assert a direct-sum decomposition, regular singularities, or a classification by arbitrary gluing matrices.
reconstruction: The circled question is resolved in the precise finite-extension sense supplied by the following finite-length and simple-object statements. “Away from curves” on a surface is not an assertion that every module has full support.
fate: The reconstruction follows the structure results read in \citet[\S\S16--17, especially Lemma 16.18 and Theorem 17.2]{gourevitch2025dmodules}; the next notebook page itself supplies these two ingredients.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Finite length of holonomic modules
notes: Theorem (15)(1) states finite length and equality of the lengths of filtrations with irreducible factors.
statement: The category of holonomic \(\mathcal D_X\)-modules on a smooth characteristic-zero algebraic variety is both noetherian and artinian. Every object admits a finite composition series; the multiset of simple factors, with multiplicities, is independent of the series.
reconstruction: The Jordan--Hölder conclusion is stated in its stronger usual form, including multiplicities rather than only length.
fate: Finite length is classical holonomic-module theory. The exact statement and its proof using duality are read in \citet[Lemma 16.18]{gourevitch2025dmodules}; compare the early finiteness framework in \citet[\S3]{bernstein1971modules}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Simple holonomic modules as minimal extensions
notes: The notes classify irreducibles by an irreducible variety and irreducible flat bundle, identify pairs after shrinking, and claim a unique irreducible submodule of \(i_*\mathcal L_Y\).
statement: Simple holonomic modules on smooth \(X\) correspond to pairs consisting of an irreducible closed support \(Z\subset X\) and an irreducible integrable connection on a nonempty smooth open subset \(U\subset Z\), modulo isomorphism after further shrinking. The corresponding module is the intermediate extension to \(X\); equivalently, it is the unique simple submodule of \(H^0j_+\mathcal L\) for the locally closed embedding \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\).
reconstruction: The connection lives on a smooth dense open subset, not necessarily all of a singular support. Equivalence is generated by restriction to a common dense open, rather than the asymmetric single inclusion written in the notes.
fate: The exact minimal-extension classification is read in \citet[Theorem 17.2]{gourevitch2025dmodules}. It is standard holonomic theory and does not require regular singularities unless one also invokes a constructible-sheaf Riemann--Hilbert equivalence.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Smoothness alone does not make a direct image simple
notes: The final line says that if \(Y\) is smooth, the direct image is already irreducible.
statement: This is valid for a closed embedding of smooth varieties and a simple source module, by Kashiwara equivalence. It is false for a general locally closed embedding: for \(j:\mathbb G_m\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1\), the simple connection \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb G_m}\) has \(j_+\mathcal O_{\mathbb G_m}=\mathcal O_{\mathbb A^1}(*0)\), which contains the proper nonzero submodule \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb A^1}\). Its quotient is supported at the origin.
reconstruction: The counterexample distinguishes smooth source from closed support and explains why intermediate extension is needed.
fate: The exact closed-embedding and intermediate-extension theorems are read in \citet[Theorems 9.1 and 17.2]{gourevitch2025dmodules}; the localization counterexample is a direct calculation in the first Weyl algebra.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Grassmannian dimension notation and coordinate inclusions
notes: The talk uses \(G_n^m\) for \(n\)-planes in \(\mathbb R^{n+m}\) and arranges coordinate inclusions in a two-dimensional array.
statement: Write \(G_n^m=\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb R^{n+m})\), of dimension \(nm\). The horizontal inclusion adds an unused coordinate; the vertical inclusion sends \(V\) to \(V\oplus\mathbb R e_{n+m+1}\). Equivalently \(G_n^m\) parametrizes projective \((n-1)\)-planes in \(\mathbb{RP}^{n+m-1}\).
reconstruction: The third entry in the second row must be \(G_2^3\), not the handwritten \(G_1^3\). These coordinate choices specify which smaller Grassmannians contain faces.
fate: The underlying coordinate Grassmannian geometry is classical; compare the explicit Grassmannian setting in \citet[pp.13--14]{atiyah1982convexity}. The table is checked directly from its dimensions.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The inadequately specified geodesic-simplex construction
notes: The opening asks for polyhedra whose faces lie in smaller Grassmannians; it says that filling a triangle with geodesic segments fails when the rank is at least two.
statement: The record does not specify a metric, a canonical filling rule, or an exact compatibility condition that is alleged to fail. Thus it records motivation for using torus orbit closures, rather than a quantified nonexistence theorem for geodesic simplices.
reconstruction: No universal claim that higher-rank Grassmannians lack totally geodesic simplices is inferred. Totally geodesic subspaces and small geodesic triangles certainly exist.
fate: The subsequent construction has a precise publication match in \citet{gelfandmacpherson1982geometry}, but no exact theorem corresponding to this preliminary objection was identified. The previous problem GP-1979-04 concerns a Grassmannian counterpart of a projective-space linear model; title-level resemblance does not establish that its exact question recurs here.
present_status: As of November 2026, this motivating remark does not determine an independently assessable mathematical problem.

title: The hypersimplex
notes: \(\Delta_n^m\) is defined by \(0\le x_i\le1\) and \(\sum x_i=n\).
statement: For positive integers \(n,m\), put \(N=n+m\) and \(\Delta(n,N)=\{x\in[0,1]^N:\sum_i x_i=n\}\). This \((N-1)\)-dimensional polytope is the convex hull of the characteristic vectors of all \(n\)-element subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\).
reconstruction: The vertex description and dimension are explicit consequences of the inequalities; \(\Delta_n^m=\Delta(n,n+m)\).
fate: The combinatorial object is classical and already occurs in 1979-486.2. Its Grassmannian realization is part of \citet{gelfandmacpherson1982geometry}; see also the read orbit-polytope theorem \citet[Theorem 2′, p.13]{atiyah1982convexity}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Positive torus orbit closures and the genericity condition
notes: A projective frame determines the identity component \(H^0\) of its stabilizer. A Grassmannian simplex is the closure of a generic orbit; generic means transverse to every coordinate subspace, not merely maximal orbit dimension.
statement: In \(\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb R^N)\), let \(H=(\mathbb R_{>0})^N/\mathbb R_{>0}\) act diagonally. If every Plücker coordinate \(p_I(V)\) is nonzero, define the Grassmannian simplex to be \(\overline{H\cdot V}\). The open orbit has dimension \(N-1\). Nonvanishing of all Plücker coordinates is stronger than maximal orbit dimension and is equivalent to the stated coordinate general-position condition.
reconstruction: The central scalar quotient, all-minor condition, and orbit closure are explicit. Non-generic supports generally yield smaller matroid polytopes, not the full hypersimplex.
fate: This is the announced Gelfand--MacPherson construction, explicitly identified by \citet[p.13]{atiyah1982convexity}. The work was published by Gelfand and MacPherson in June 1982; this 9 February 1981 seminar is a verified earlier oral occurrence. No earlier public preprint date was independently established.
present_status: As of November 2026, this construction is established. The distinction between full Plücker support and maximal orbit dimension remains essential.

title: The orbit closure is a hypersimplex with its face stratification
notes: P000950 calls the two objects diffeomorphic; P000952 identifies face interiors with positive-torus orbits, and P000953 corrects the global conclusion to homeomorphism with smoothness on individual orbits.
statement: For the generic \(V\) above, the Grassmannian moment map restricts to a homeomorphism \(\overline{H\cdot V}\to\Delta(n,N)\). One convenient expression is \(\mu(V)=\sum_I |p_I(V)|^2\mathbf1_I/\sum_I|p_I(V)|^2\). Each positive orbit maps diffeomorphically to a relative face interior. A global diffeomorphism of embedded orbit closures is not asserted; boundary strata can be singular.
reconstruction: The corrected conclusion follows the notebook's own later qualification. The formula fixes the normalization and makes the polytope correspondence concrete.
fate: \citet[Theorems 2 and 2′, pp.3 and 13]{atiyah1982convexity} proves the exact orbit-closure statement and explicitly identifies the real-Grassmannian case with Gelfand--MacPherson. The work was published by Gelfand and MacPherson in June 1982; this 9 February 1981 seminar is a verified earlier oral occurrence. No earlier public preprint date was independently established.
present_status: As of November 2026, the homeomorphism and orbit-by-face smoothness are established; the initial unrestricted diffeomorphism wording requires the recorded correction.

title: The projective triangle and its dual Grassmannian triangle
notes: The examples \(G_1^2\) and \(G_2^1\) give four triangular chambers in the projective plane and a dual triangle of lines, with sides in \(G_1^1\).
statement: The complement of the three coordinate lines in \(\mathbb{RP}^2\) has four sign chambers, each a positive diagonal orbit; its closure is a triangle. Dually, two-planes in \(\mathbb R^3\) are kernels of nonzero covectors, and each covector-sign chamber similarly gives a triangle. Its edges consist of planes containing a fixed coordinate axis, and its vertices are coordinate two-planes.
reconstruction: The dual description depends on the selected sign chamber. The informal phrase about lines avoiding a hatched region is interpreted through these explicit coordinate conditions.
fate: These elementary models are exact special cases of the orbit-closure construction; \citet[Theorem 2′]{atiyah1982convexity}. They are already implicit in the earlier configuration descriptions 1979-487.1--2.
present_status: As of November 2026, the coordinate and dual models are established; the drawings specify a chosen chamber, not the whole dual projective plane.

title: The octahedron and the cross-ratio in Gr(2,4)
notes: \(G_2^2\) is four-dimensional, its positive orbit is three-dimensional, and the cross-ratio of four planes through a projective line is constant along the orbit. The six vertices are labelled by pairs.
statement: For a generic projective line \(\ell\subset\mathbb{RP}^3\), the planes spanned by \(\ell\) and the four coordinate points determine four distinct points in the projective line of planes through \(\ell\). Their cross-ratio is invariant under diagonal transformations. The positive-orbit closure is \(\Delta(2,4)\), an octahedron with six pair-labelled vertices and eight triangular facets, four of each coordinate-facet type.
reconstruction: Cross-ratio conventions and sign chambers must be fixed to identify a particular connected orbit in a level set; the notes state only containment in a level set.
fate: This is the same four-ray/cross-ratio geometry discussed in 1979-486.12--13. The hypersimplex identification follows the exact theorem read in \citet[Theorem 2′]{atiyah1982convexity}; its use in the dilogarithm construction was published in \citet{gelfandmacpherson1982geometry}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the octahedral model and cross-ratio invariant are established.

title: Dilogarithmic volume between two Grassmannian simplices
notes: The recorded volume between \(K=c_1\) and \(K=c_2\), with \(0<c_1<c_2<1\), is \(\Phi(c_1)-\Phi(c_2)\), where \(\Phi(x)=\operatorname{Li}_2(x)-\operatorname{Li}_2(1-x)\).
statement: The formula can describe an oriented, normalized characteristic-form integral, but it cannot literally be an unsigned positive volume with the stated order: \(\Phi^{\prime}(x)=-\log(1-x)/x-\log x/(1-x)>0\). The natural increasing primitive satisfies \(\Phi=2L-\pi^2/6\), where \(L(x)=\operatorname{Li}_2(x)+\tfrac12\log x\log(1-x)\) is the Rogers dilogarithm. An unsigned volume requires the opposite difference after fixing the form normalization.
reconstruction: The sign test is direct. The exact normalization of the invariant four-form, orientation of the slab, and choice of cross-ratio are not recoverable from this line alone, so no numerical constant is silently supplied.
fate: The geometric dilogarithm construction is the subject of \citet{gelfandmacpherson1982geometry}; publisher metadata is verified, but its full text was not retrieved. The precise Rogers identity and normalization are read in \citet[Chapter II, \S1.A]{zagier2007dilogarithm}. The work was published by Gelfand and MacPherson in June 1982; this 9 February 1981 seminar is a verified earlier oral occurrence. No earlier public preprint date was independently established.
present_status: As of November 2026, the characteristic-form/dilogarithm construction is established, but the notebook's unsigned-volume wording has a sign defect and omits normalization.

title: The two families of hypersimplex boundary faces
notes: Equation (12) starts an alternating boundary sum over \(x_i=0\) faces and then breaks off in the second family; its second lower limit is written \(-1\).
statement: For \(1<n<N-1\), the facets of \(\Delta(n,N)\) are \(x_i=0\), isomorphic to \(\Delta(n,N-1)\), and \(x_i=1\), isomorphic to \(\Delta(n-1,N-1)\). Giving the ambient affine hyperplane and each facet compatible orientations yields its ordinary signed cellular boundary. At \(n=1\) or \(n=N-1\), the degenerate family must be omitted as a family of facets.
reconstruction: The missing \(x_i=1\) condition and index range \(i=1,\ldots,N\) are reconstructed from the defining inequalities. The incomplete manuscript does not determine a fully checked orientation-sign formula.
fate: The face geometry is elementary and underlies \citet{gelfandmacpherson1982geometry}; the face/orbit compatibility is independently read in \citet[Theorem 2]{atiyah1982convexity}. No unverified completion of the alternating signs is represented as a transcription.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Vanishing of harmonic forms on real Grassmannian simplices
notes: Equation (13) claims that every harmonic form on \(G_n^m\), for a coordinate-compatible metric, vanishes on every Grassmannian simplex.
statement: For the unoriented real Grassmannian \(G_n^m\) with \(nm\) even and its orthogonally invariant metric, every harmonic differential form of positive degree restricts to zero on each positive diagonal orbit. The same assertion holds for the corresponding invariant positive-degree forms. Constants are excluded; the unrestricted assertion fails in general for \(nm\) odd and for oriented Grassmannians.
reconstruction: Positive degree, the unoriented space, and the parity hypothesis are supplied from the primary theorem. Restriction is understood on the smooth orbit strata, avoiding a fictitious smooth structure at singular boundary points.
fate: \citet[pp.13--14, discussion before and after Theorem 4]{atiyah1982convexity} states this Gelfand--MacPherson result, gives a new proof, and explicitly records the odd-dimensional and oriented failures. The work was published by Gelfand and MacPherson in June 1982; this 9 February 1981 seminar is a verified earlier oral occurrence. No earlier public preprint date was independently established.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified vanishing theorem is established; the literal all-degrees, all-Grassmannians formulation is false.

title: Five configurations and the differential five-term identity
notes: Five points on \(\mathbb P^1\), modulo projectivities, form a two-dimensional space. Omitting each point gives a cross-ratio \(k_i\), and equation (14) alternates the differentials \(d\Phi(k_i)\).
statement: The moduli space of five ordered distinct points on \(\mathbb P^1\) modulo \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\) has dimension two. On a real chamber with consistent cross-ratio conventions, the five-term relation is equivalent to the Rogers identity, for \(0<x,y<1\): \[L(x)+L(y)=L(xy)+L\!\left(\frac{x(1-y)}{1-xy}\right)+L\!\left(\frac{y(1-x)}{1-xy}\right).\] Since \(\Phi=2L-\pi^2/6\), differentiating gives a five-term zero relation; its displayed signs depend on the ordered cross-ratios.
reconstruction: A concrete branch-free chamber and the exact five arguments replace the notebook's unspecified cross-ratio convention. The constant in the corresponding undifferentiated \(\Phi\)-relation is \(\pi^2/6\).
fate: The analytic identity is classical, not new in 1981; its exact Rogers form is read in \citet[Chapter II, \S1.A]{zagier2007dilogarithm}. The geometric derivation is the Gelfand--MacPherson contribution discussed separately below.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Pontryagin-form fibre integration and Stokes’ formula
notes: The notes use the first Pontryagin form on \(G_3^2\), say its harmonic degree-four space is one-dimensional, and apply fibre integration with boundary terms over the space of five-point configurations.
statement: The invariant degree-four cohomology of \(\operatorname{Gr}_3(\mathbb R^5)\) is one-dimensional, generated by the first Pontryagin class of the tautological bundle (equivalently the negative of the quotient bundle class). On the suitable oriented family of compactified positive orbits, fibre integration of its closed invariant representative satisfies the Stokes formula with oriented facet terms. The vanishing theorem and the two facet families turn those terms into the differential five-term identity.
reconstruction: The tautological rank-three and complementary rank-two bundles have opposite first Pontryagin classes because their sum is trivial. “Exactly one form” means a one-dimensional vector space. Boundary orientations and the family compactification must be fixed; the abbreviated diagram does not supply them.
fate: This is a recurrence of the characteristic-form construction in 1979-486.14--15 and 1979-487.2, published in \citet{gelfandmacpherson1982geometry}. The exact vanishing input is independently read in \citet[Theorem 4 and its Grassmannian application]{atiyah1982convexity}. Full verification of every 1982 normalization was unavailable.
present_status: As of November 2026, the geometric mechanism is established; this occurrence does not fix a unique sign and normalization for the primitive.

title: Positive orbits in compact Kähler manifolds and their polytope closures
notes: The generalization says that algebraic torus actions with a fixed point have positive-real orbits homeomorphic to polyhedra, with only stratumwise differentiability.
statement: Let a compact torus \(T\) act by Kähler automorphisms on a compact connected Kähler manifold \(M\), with a fixed point. Let \(T^{\mathbb C}=T\cdot H\), where \(\operatorname{Lie}H=J\operatorname{Lie}T\), and choose a moment map. For each \(y\), the moment map restricts to a homeomorphism \(\overline{H\cdot y}\to P_y\), a convex polytope; \(H\cdot y\) maps to its relative interior, and lower orbits to face interiors.
reconstruction: Compactness, a Kähler-preserving action, and an orbit closure are supplied. A positive orbit itself is generally noncompact and cannot be homeomorphic to a compact polytope.
fate: This is the exact general theorem of \citet[Theorems 2 and 2′]{atiyah1982convexity}, published in 1982 after receipt on 27 March 1981. The notebook's 9 February report is earlier evidence of oral circulation; receipt is not treated as a public preprint date.
present_status: As of November 2026, the orbit-closure theorem is established with the compact Kähler and Hamiltonian hypotheses.

title: Kähler harmonic-form vanishing on the positive torus part
notes: A torus-invariant harmonic form, with respect to a Kähler metric, is said to vanish on every positive-real orbit.
statement: For compact connected Kähler \(M\), a torus \(T\) preserving its Kähler structure and having a fixed point, every harmonic form of degree \(\ell>0\) restricts to zero on the orbits of the positive subgroup \(H\subset T^{\mathbb C}\). A torus orbit is null-homotopic through the fixed point; its invariant exact pullback vanishes, and Hodge-type decomposition transfers this conclusion from \(T\)-directions to \(J T\)-directions.
reconstruction: The degree-zero exception and the compact connected hypotheses are explicit. A \(T\)-invariant Kähler metric ensures the form-invariance used in the proof.
fate: The statement and proof are read in \citet[Theorem 4, pp.13--14]{atiyah1982convexity}. The paper appeared in 1982; its recorded receipt was 27 March 1981, after this seminar report.
present_status: As of November 2026, the positive-degree theorem is established; nonzero harmonic constants are the immediate exception to the literal wording.

title: Convexity for commuting Hamiltonians and the orbit-image conflation
notes: Theorem (15), attributed to Atiyah, assumes Poisson commutation and a common critical point, then depicts an orbit of the Hamiltonian fields mapping to a convex polyhedron.
statement: Let \(M\) be compact connected symplectic and \(f_1,\ldots,f_r\) commuting Hamiltonians whose flows generate a compact torus action (Atiyah allows almost-periodic fields). The map \(f:M\to\mathbb R^r\) has connected nonempty fibres and convex-polytope image, the convex hull of its common critical values. Its restriction to an orbit of the Hamiltonian fields is constant, since \(H_{f_i}(f_j)=\{f_i,f_j\}=0\). Nontrivial orbit polytopes instead concern the positive complexified action in the Kähler version.
reconstruction: The missing compactness and almost-periodicity hypotheses and the correct domain of the moment-image assertion are supplied. Mere commutation plus a common critical point is insufficient: on a symplectic two-torus, \((\cos x,\cos^2x)\) has these properties and a nonconvex parabolic image.
fate: The full theorem is read in \citet[Theorem 1 and following remarks, pp.2--3]{atiyah1982convexity}; the orbit theorem is its distinct Theorem 2′. Publication was 1982, receipt 27 March 1981. The counterexample and constant-orbit observation are direct checks here.
present_status: As of November 2026, moment-map convexity is established. The notebook conflates the whole-manifold moment image, positive complexified orbits, and Hamiltonian orbits; the latter have point images.
