title: Genus of a hyperelliptic curve
notes: The motivating example is \(y^2=P_n(x)\), with \(P_n\) squarefree, and genus \(\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\); degrees three and four give one handle and degrees five and six give two.
statement: Over \(\mathbb C\), let \(P\) be a squarefree polynomial of degree \(n\geq1\). The smooth projective model of \(y^2=P(x)\) has genus \(\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\). Indeed, its degree-two map to \(\mathbb P^1\) has \(n\) finite simple branch points and one further branch point at infinity exactly when \(n\) is odd; Riemann--Hurwitz gives the formula.
reconstruction: The genus belongs to the smooth compact model. The branch count supplies an elementary proof and includes the point at infinity.
fate: This is a classical hyperelliptic genus calculation. It also follows from the Newton-polygon genus theorem read in \citet[\S2]{khovanskii1978genus}; that publication predates this explanatory talk.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Degree genus formula and why the hyperelliptic plane model is special
notes: The notes give \((n-1)(n-2)/2\) for a general degree-\(n\) equation, then say that the hyperelliptic equation is “not an equation of degree \(n\)”.
statement: A nonsingular plane projective curve of degree \(d\) has genus \((d-1)(d-2)/2\). For \(n\geq2\), \(y^2-P_n(x)\) does have total degree \(n\); its projective closure is a special degree-\(n\) model, generally singular at infinity, so the nonsingular plane-curve formula cannot simply be applied to that model.
reconstruction: The intended distinction is generic versus special support, not total degree. Passing to normalization explains the discrepancy in genera.
fate: This is the classical plane genus formula. Its realization as the count of interior lattice points of the degree-\(d\) triangle is covered by \citet[\S2]{khovanskii1978genus} and the speaker's later explicit comparison in \citet[slides 6--8]{khovanskii2025chern}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Newton polygons and Laurent-monomial translation
notes: The Newton polygon is the convex hull of exponent pairs with nonzero coefficients. Multiplication by \(x^ay^b\) translates it; the curve is considered away from the coordinate cross.
statement: For a nonzero Laurent polynomial \(P=\sum_{m\in A}c_mx^m\) on \(T=(\mathbb C^*)^n\), define \(\Delta(P)=\operatorname{conv}\{m:c_m\ne0\}\subset\mathbb R^n\). Since a Laurent monomial is a unit on \(T\), multiplying by it leaves the torus zero scheme unchanged and translates \(\Delta(P)\) by the exponent vector.
reconstruction: The torus restriction is essential: multiplication by a polynomial monomial can add coordinate-axis components in affine space.
fate: The definition and its character-lattice interpretation are read in \citet[\S\S1--2]{khovanskii1977toroidal}, published in 1977. These are already established tools in the 1981 lecture.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The Newton-polygon genus theorem
notes: The answer to the first motivating question is the number of interior lattice points of the Newton polygon, for coefficients in general position; the notebook attributes the earlier result to Baker and its rediscovery to Khovanskii.
statement: Let \(P\in\mathbb C[x^{\pm1},y^{\pm1}]\) have a two-dimensional Newton polygon \(\Delta\), and assume its torus curve is irreducible and Newton nondegenerate: for every face \(F\), including \(\Delta\), the equations \(P_F=x\partial_xP_F=y\partial_yP_F=0\) have no common solution in \((\mathbb C^*)^2\). The genus of its smooth projective model is \(\#(\operatorname{int}\Delta\cap\mathbb Z^2)\). Generic coefficients with prescribed full Newton polygon satisfy these hypotheses.
reconstruction: Face nondegeneracy and the smooth projective model make “general position” precise. The historical teacher--student anecdote is not needed for the theorem and was not independently verified.
fate: The exact hypersurface genus result is read in \citet[\S2]{khovanskii1978genus}; its companion paper \citet[\S2]{khovanskii1977toroidal} defines nondegeneracy and the good toric compactification. Thus the talk is exposition of published 1977--1978 work, not a new unresolved genus question.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Boundary valuations and unimodular monomial changes
notes: At an omitted point, the orders of \(x,y\) give an integral vector. A monomial substitution with determinant one changes this vector by the corresponding integral matrix; primitive vectors can be made coordinate vectors.
statement: On the smooth compactification of an irreducible torus curve, each boundary point \(p\) has \(v_p=(\operatorname{ord}_p x,\operatorname{ord}_p y)\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{0\}\). Under \(x=u^{a_{11}}v^{a_{12}},\ y=u^{a_{21}}v^{a_{22}}\), the order column is multiplied by \(A\). For \(A\in\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)\), the map is an isomorphism of tori. Any primitive lattice vector is carried to a coordinate vector by such a matrix. In the nondegenerate compactification the boundary order vectors are primitive inward edge normals.
reconstruction: The determinant may be either \(1\) or \(-1\); the written determinant-one subcase is sufficient. Primitivity of boundary vectors uses transverse intersection with the toric boundary and cannot be assumed for arbitrary singular curves.
fate: The lattice duality and admissible smooth toric charts are read in \citet[\S1]{khovanskii1977toroidal}; its \S2 gives the transverse compactification for nondegenerate systems.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Edge lengths count punctures
notes: After translating an edge to a coordinate axis, its polynomial has as many nonzero roots as the length of the edge, with distinct roots in general position. A later sentence instead says “number of lattice points on the segment”; the total puncture count is the number of boundary lattice points.
statement: Under the nondegeneracy hypotheses of 1980-509.4, the compactified curve meets the toric divisor associated to an edge \(E\) in exactly its lattice length \(\ell(E)=\#(E\cap\mathbb Z^2)-1\) distinct transverse points. Consequently the number of punctures of the curve in \((\mathbb C^*)^2\) is \(\sum_E\ell(E)=\#(\partial\Delta\cap\mathbb Z^2)\). Vertex initial polynomials are monomials and contribute no roots.
reconstruction: The local edge count and the global boundary-point count differ by one per closed edge because vertices are counted twice in the latter edgewise listing. Simple roots supply the transverse local parameter.
fate: This is the elementary boundary calculation in the nondegenerate toric compactification of \citet[\S\S1--2]{khovanskii1977toroidal}; the speaker states the exact curve count again in \citet[slide 6]{khovanskii2025chern}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Divisor degree and the signed boundary root count
notes: The notes restrict \(Q\) to \(P=0\), say its divisor is zero, substitute \(x\sim t^n,y\sim t^m\), and sum minimum scalar products over punctures to count the torus roots.
statement: Let \(C\) be the smooth projective model of \(P=0\) and let \(Q|_C\) be a nonzero meromorphic function. Then \(\deg\operatorname{div}(Q|_C)=0\), not generally \(\operatorname{div}(Q|_C)=0\). If the initial terms of \(Q\) do not cancel at a boundary point \(p\), its order is \(\min_{a\in\Delta(Q)}\langle a,v_p\rangle\). As \(Q\) has no poles in the torus, the number of its torus zeros, with multiplicity, is \[-\sum_{p\in C\setminus T}\operatorname{ord}_p(Q)=-\sum_{p\in C\setminus T}\min_{a\in\Delta(Q)}\langle a,v_p\rangle.\]
reconstruction: The missing minus sign and the difference between a divisor and its degree are explicit corrections. Local expansions have nonvanishing unit factors and the right-hand side of equation (11) requires the full sum; the minimum formula needs noncancellation of its leading coefficient.
fate: The valuation and intersection mechanism is already present in \citet[\S\S1--2]{khovanskii1977toroidal} and the root-count application in \citet[\S1]{khovanskii1978genus}. The sign is checked directly from the degree-zero identity.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Mixed area and the two incompatible normalizations
notes: The planar coefficient \(S(K,L)\) is defined by \(\operatorname{Area}(aK+bL)=a^2\operatorname{Area}(K)+b^2\operatorname{Area}(L)+abS(K,L)\). The following general definition instead sets \(V(K,\ldots,K)=\operatorname{Vol}(K)\).
statement: The standard mixed volume is the symmetric Minkowski-multilinear functional with \(V(K,\ldots,K)=\operatorname{Vol}_n(K)\); equivalently, the coefficient of \(t_1\cdots t_n\) in \(\operatorname{Vol}(\sum t_iK_i)\) is \(n!V(K_1,\ldots,K_n)\). Thus \(S(K,L)=2V(K,L)=\operatorname{Area}(K+L)-\operatorname{Area}(K)-\operatorname{Area}(L)\), and \(S(K,K)=2\operatorname{Area}(K)\).
reconstruction: Symmetry and multilinearity in every slot are included in the characterization. The notebook shifts from the coefficient normalization \(S\) to the diagonal-volume normalization \(V\), so they cannot be substituted into root counts without the factorial.
fate: The exact polarization normalization is read in \citet[\S1, mixed-volume definition]{khovanskii1978genus} and \citet[slide 12]{khovanskii2025chern}. This is classical mixed-volume theory; the later lecture is an explicit normalization check.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Bernshtein’s torus root count, with multiplicities and nondegeneracy
notes: The second motivating question is answered by mixed area, and theorem (14), attributed to D. Bernshtein, states the generic system root count as the mixed volume of its Newton polytopes.
statement: For finite supports \(A_i\subset\mathbb Z^n\), put \(\Delta_i=\operatorname{conv}(A_i)\). A generic system of Laurent polynomials \(f_i\) with these Newton polytopes has \(n!V(\Delta_1,\ldots,\Delta_n)\) isolated roots in \((\mathbb C^*)^n\), counted with multiplicity. A sufficient precise hypothesis for equality is that for every nonzero weight \(w\in\mathbb R^n\), the simultaneous initial system \(f_{1,w}=\cdots=f_{n,w}=0\) has no torus root and that the original system is zero-dimensional. In two variables the count is \(S(\Delta(P),\Delta(Q))\).
reconstruction: The torus, multiplicities, finite intersection, and nonzero-weight conditions are explicit. With the normalization immediately preceding theorem (14), its right-hand side lacks \(n!\), or lacks \(2\) in the stated planar case.
fate: \citet{bernshtein1975roots} was published in 1975 (received 7 April 1975; receipt is not a public-circulation date). The exact normalized theorem is read in \citet[\S1, number-of-solutions consequence]{khovanskii1978genus}. It is therefore known before this talk. Earlier 1974 Newton-polyhedron occurrences concern local singularity invariants and are not automatically the same problem.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Equal polygons and the Bézout specialization
notes: When both polygons coincide, a support-distance sum equals twice their area; for the degree triangle this gives \(n^2\), identified with Bézout.
statement: Two generic torus polynomials with the same Newton polygon \(\Delta\) have \(2\operatorname{Area}(\Delta)\) common roots. For generic polynomials of total degrees \(d,e\), the polygons are \(d\Sigma,e\Sigma\), where \(\Sigma=\operatorname{conv}(0,e_1,e_2)\); hence the mixed-area root count is \(de\). Genericity ensures that the projective Bézout intersections do not escape to coordinate divisors.
reconstruction: The displayed \(n^2\) is the equal-degree subcase. The support-distance formula is invariant under translation because the length-weighted outward normals sum to zero.
fate: This is the classical Bézout count recovered from the already published Bernshtein theorem; see \citet[\S1]{khovanskii1978genus}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Euler characteristic of a nondegenerate torus hypersurface
notes: The word “curve” is crossed out in favor of “hypersurface”, while equation (15) retains the constant negative sign \(-n!\operatorname{Vol}(\Delta)\).
statement: Let \(f\) have full-dimensional Newton polytope \(\Delta\subset\mathbb R^n\), and assume every face truncation, including the full polynomial, defines a smooth hypersurface in \((\mathbb C^*)^n\) when nonempty. Then \[\chi\{f=0\text{ in }(\mathbb C^*)^n\}=(-1)^{n-1}n!\operatorname{Vol}_n(\Delta).\] For complex algebraic varieties the ordinary and compactly supported Euler characteristics agree, although their cohomology groups do not generally agree.
reconstruction: The parity-dependent sign and the nondegeneracy assumption are supplied. The negative sign is correct for plane torus curves, but already fails for one-variable polynomials, whose zero set has positive cardinality.
fate: The exact result is read in \citet[\S3, Theorem 2 and hypersurface example]{khovanskii1978genus}. It was published three years before the seminar occurrence.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Pick’s formula from genus, punctures, and Euler characteristic
notes: Combining \(\chi=2-2B-\Gamma=-2S\), with \(B\) interior and \(\Gamma\) boundary lattice points, gives \(B+\Gamma/2=S+1\).
statement: For a two-dimensional convex lattice polygon \(\Delta\), write \(I=\#(\operatorname{int}\Delta\cap\mathbb Z^2)\) and \(B=\#(\partial\Delta\cap\mathbb Z^2)\). Then \(\operatorname{Area}(\Delta)=I+B/2-1\). Choosing a generic nondegenerate torus curve gives genus \(I\), exactly \(B\) punctures, and Euler characteristic \(-2\operatorname{Area}(\Delta)\), which proves the identity.
reconstruction: Notation distinguishes the notebook's area \(S\) from its mixed-area coefficient. A generic curve exists for any such polygon; the formula is for the polygon itself.
fate: Pick's identity is classical. The same algebraic derivation is explicitly presented by the speaker in \citet[slides 6--7]{khovanskii2025chern}, and its ingredients were already published in \citet{khovanskii1978genus}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Mixed area with a disk and the isoperimetric inequality
notes: The mixed area of a polygon and the unit disk is its perimeter. The following inequality is written in the diagonal-volume normalization, \(V(K,L)^2\geq\operatorname{Area}(K)\operatorname{Area}(L)\), and equality for a disk is mentioned.
statement: For compact convex planar bodies \(K,L\) with nonempty interior, \(V(K,L)^2\geq\operatorname{Area}(K)\operatorname{Area}(L)\). If \(B\) is the unit disk, \(2V(K,B)=\operatorname{Perimeter}(K)\), because \(\operatorname{Area}(K+tB)=\operatorname{Area}(K)+t\operatorname{Perimeter}(K)+\pi t^2\). Hence \(\operatorname{Perimeter}(K)^2\geq4\pi\operatorname{Area}(K)\), with equality for disks.
reconstruction: The notebook's perimeter statement uses its coefficient normalization \(S=2V\). This accounts for the factor of four in the isoperimetric inequality; convexity and full planar dimension are explicit.
fate: These are established Minkowski and isoperimetric inequalities, not questions left open in 1981. The precise normalization and disk consequence are read in \citet[slide 12]{khovanskii2025chern}; the general Alexandrov--Fenchel statement is read in \citet[Theorem 2.1]{kavehkhovanskii2012equations}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The surface intersection inequality requires positivity
notes: For any two curves on any algebraic surface the notes claim \((\Gamma_1\cdot\Gamma_2)^2\geq\Gamma_1^2\Gamma_2^2\), citing the Hodge structure and relating it to mixed area.
statement: On a smooth projective complex surface, nef real divisor classes \(D,E\) satisfy \((D\cdot E)^2\geq D^2E^2\), by the Hodge index theorem and approximation by ample classes. The assertion for arbitrary curves is false: the two disjoint exceptional curves on the blow-up of \(\mathbb P^2\) at two distinct points have squares \(-1\) and mutual intersection zero. For globally generated toric divisors associated to polygons, \(D_K\cdot D_L=2V(K,L)\), which gives the mixed-area inequality.
reconstruction: Smoothness, projectivity, and positivity are substantive hypotheses. The exceptional-curve example is a direct diagnostic counterexample, not a historical attribution. The last toric identity requires a common smooth projective refinement of the polygons' normal fans.
fate: The surface Hodge inequality is classical. The exact positive-form version and its proof are read in \citet[Corollary 7.11]{kavehkhovanskii2010mixed}; the same paper explains the toric intersection/mixed-volume correspondence in \S2. The later work broadens the intersection theory but does not make the unrestricted notebook assertion true.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Toric compactification from compatible monomial charts
notes: The end of the talk begins a compactification by monomial changes of coordinates and cones, explaining how a curve or divisor becomes visible at the boundary.
statement: A finite fan \(\Sigma\) of strongly convex rational polyhedral cones in the cocharacter lattice defines a normal toric variety by gluing \(U_\sigma=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[\sigma^\vee\cap M]\) along their face charts. When every cone is generated by part of a lattice basis, the variety is smooth. A complete fan gives a compact complex toric variety. Refining the normal fan of the Newton polytopes supplies a compactification in which nondegenerate complete intersections meet torus strata transversely.
reconstruction: Compatibility means that every cone intersection is a common face and all faces are included; mere disjointness of maximal-cone interiors does not suffice. The later 23 February occurrence supplies the fuller chart and completeness discussion.
fate: The exact construction and admissibility/completeness theorems are read in \citet[\S1]{khovanskii1977toroidal}, and the systematic fan construction in \citet[\S5]{danilov1978toric}. Both sources were explicitly available before this lecture.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Unimodular torus charts and character--cocharacter duality
notes: The continuation writes \(x_i=\prod_j u_j^{a_{ij}}\), one-parameter groups \(x_i=t^{\lambda_i}\), and the value \(t^{\langle m,\lambda\rangle}\) of a monomial on such a group.
statement: For \(T=(\mathbb C^*)^n\), the character lattice \(M=\operatorname{Hom}(T,\mathbb C^*)\) and cocharacter lattice \(N=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb C^*,T)\) are dual. In chosen bases, \(\chi^m(t^\lambda)=t^{\langle m,\lambda\rangle}\). The monomial change \(x_i=\prod_j u_j^{a_{ij}}\) is an isomorphism of tori precisely when \(A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb Z)\). An \(\mathbb A^n\) chart in a smooth toric compactification corresponds to a maximal cone generated by its cocharacter-basis columns.
reconstruction: Unimodularity distinguishes a chart isomorphism from a finite monomial covering. The statement concerns a chosen torus with its action, not arbitrary analytic compactifications.
fate: The exact pairing, monomial coordinate change, and associated cones are read in \citet[\S1]{khovanskii1977toroidal}, published in 1977, and \citet[\S5]{danilov1978toric}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The fan compatibility condition
notes: Cones are generated by the columns of the chart matrix. Overlapping interiors force equality; a second statement applies the same requirement to faces.
statement: A finite collection of strongly convex rational cones defines a separated toric gluing when it is closed under faces and the intersection of every two cones is a face of each. Equivalently, relative interiors of all its cones are disjoint unless the cones coincide. Smoothness requires every cone to be generated by part of a lattice basis.
reconstruction: The second, facewise sentence is essential: disjoint interiors of maximal cones alone are insufficient. Including all faces makes the notebook's criterion the standard fan condition.
fate: This is the admissibility theorem in \citet[\S1]{khovanskii1977toroidal}; compare the systematic fan gluing in \citet[\S5]{danilov1978toric}. It is established before the lecture.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The sigma-process example is one blow-up chart
notes: The substitution \(x_1=u_1u_2^{-1},\ x_2=u_2\), or \(u_1=x_1x_2,\ u_2=x_2\), is called a sigma-process.
statement: The map \((x_1,x_2)\mapsto(u_1,u_2)=(x_1x_2,x_2)\) is one affine chart of the blow-up of the origin in the \(u\)-plane; the other standard chart is needed for the complete blow-up. Torically, the modification subdivides the positive-quadrant cone by the ray \(e_1+e_2\). On the dense torus the displayed inverse is the stated unimodular monomial transformation.
reconstruction: The direction of the morphism and the need for the second chart are explicit; the inverse formula is not regular along \(u_2=0\) in the original plane.
fate: The standard toric modification construction is read in \citet[\S5 and the discussion of subdivisions]{danilov1978toric}; its unimodular chart interpretation is also in \citet[\S1]{khovanskii1977toroidal}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Completeness, the projective-plane fan, and toric classification
notes: The compactness criterion is that the cones cover the whole vector space. A three-ray drawing gives the projective plane, and the compactification is said to be determined up to an integral automorphism.
statement: The complex toric variety \(X_\Sigma\) is complete (equivalently compact analytically) exactly when \(|\Sigma|=N_\mathbb R\). The fan with rays \((1,0),(0,1),(-1,-1)\) and the three intervening two-dimensional cones gives \(\mathbb P^2\). Smooth complete toric varieties with their dense torus action are classified by smooth complete fans; allowing an automorphism of the torus identifies fans under \(\operatorname{GL}(N)\). Completeness alone does not assert projectivity.
reconstruction: The classification is equivariant and concerns valid fans. The projective-plane ray generators are reconstructed from the standard three-chart model shown schematically.
fate: The completeness equivalence is read in \citet[\S1, compactness theorem]{khovanskii1977toroidal}; \citet[\S5]{danilov1978toric} supplies the fan classification. Both precede 1981.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Exponential sums and complex Newton polytopes
notes: The proposed extension replaces Laurent polynomials by finite sums \(f(z)=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}c_\lambda e^{\langle z,\lambda\rangle}\), with \(\Lambda\subset\mathbb C^n\), and calls \(\operatorname{conv}(\Lambda)\) the Newton polyhedron.
statement: For a finite spectrum \(\Lambda\subset(\mathbb C^n)^*\), with nonzero coefficients on its support, the expression defines an entire exponential sum. Its complex Newton polytope is the real convex hull \(\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{2n}\) of that spectrum. The pairing in the exponential is complex bilinear; the associated real support function is \(h_\Gamma(z)=\max_{\lambda\in\Gamma}\operatorname{Re}\langle z,\lambda\rangle\). Integer real spectra recover Laurent polynomials after \(x_j=e^{z_j}\).
reconstruction: The real convex hull and the complex-bilinear pairing are distinguished. The logarithmic substitution is a covering map, so it changes finite torus counts into densities of infinitely many lifted roots.
fate: The definition is read at the opening of \citet[p.347]{kazarnovskii1981zeros}. The paper appeared in 1981 and records receipt on 6 November 1980; receipt is not treated as evidence of public circulation. The seminar report on 23 February 1981 is the verified oral occurrence.
present_status: As of November 2026, the complex-spectrum formulation is established; it is the precise setting of the announced extension.

title: Asymptotic zero count for regular exponential systems
notes: For \(F=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)\), the notebook states \(N_F(R)=cV(\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_n)R^n+O(R^{n-1})\), without recording the regularity condition or exact constant.
statement: Put \(\Gamma=\sum_i\Gamma_i\). For each face \(\Delta\) of \(\Gamma\), write \(\Delta=\sum_i\Delta_i\) and form the face sums \(f_i^\Delta\). Assume there is \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for every face whose complex affine span has dimension less than \(n\), and every \(z\in\mathbb C^n\), \[\sum_i\frac{|f_i^\Delta(z)|}{\max_{\lambda\in\Lambda_i\cap\Delta_i}|e^{\langle z,\lambda\rangle}|}\geq\varepsilon.\] This is Kazarnovskii's regularity condition. Counting isolated common roots with multiplicity in the radius-\(R\) Euclidean ball, \[N_F(R)=\frac{\kappa_n n!}{(2\pi)^n}P_n(\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_n)R^n+O(R^{n-1}),\] where \(\kappa_n\) is the volume of the real unit \(n\)-ball and \(P_n\) agrees with ordinary mixed volume for bodies in \(\mathbb R^n\).
reconstruction: The condition and normalization are imported from the publication. A system with common positive-dimensional zero components cannot be counted by the literal bare formula. For \(e^z-1\), \(P_1([0,1])=1\) gives \(N(R)=R/\pi+O(1)\), checking the constant. The actual notebook scan clearly has uppercase \(O\); the retrieved 1981 OCR renders that glyph ambiguously.
fate: This matches \citet[Definition 3 and Theorem 1, pp.348--349]{kazarnovskii1981zeros}, specialized to \(r=n\). The paper appeared in 1981 and records receipt on 6 November 1980; receipt is not treated as evidence of public circulation. The seminar report on 23 February 1981 is the verified oral occurrence.
present_status: As of November 2026, the stated regular-system asymptotic is established. No claim is made for an arbitrary fixed system with the same spectra.

title: The face formula for pseudovolume
notes: The diagonal functional is a sum over real \(n\)-faces of volume times external angle times the area distortion of \(E^\perp\to iE\).
statement: For a convex polytope \(\Gamma\subset\mathbb C^n\), \[P_n(\Gamma)=\sum_{\dim_{\mathbb R} F=n}\operatorname{Vol}_n(F)\,\Omega(F)\,g(E_F),\qquad g(E)=\left|\det\bigl(\operatorname{pr}_{iE}|_{E^\perp}\bigr)\right|.\] Here \(E_F\) is the direction space of the face, and \(\Omega(F)\) is the solid angle of its exterior normal cone, normalized as a fraction of the unit ball in \(E_F^\perp\). In particular \(g(\mathbb R^n)=1\), while \(g(E)=0\) when \(E\) contains a complex line. The formula is unitarily invariant; for \(n>1\) it is not generally monotone under inclusion.
reconstruction: All face dimensions are real; the determinant is an absolute Euclidean Jacobian between equal-dimensional real spaces. For a lower-dimensional body its whole body can be a face and its normal cone can be a full orthogonal space.
fate: The exact face construction, complex-angle factor, and nonmonotonicity warning are read in \citet[\S1, Definition 1]{kazarnovskii1981zeros}. The notebook's projection is the transpose version of the same equal-dimensional projection determinant. The paper appeared in 1981 and records receipt on 6 November 1980; receipt is not treated as evidence of public circulation. The seminar report on 23 February 1981 is the verified oral occurrence.
present_status: As of November 2026, the face formula and its Hermitian dependence are established; ordinary real volume is only a special case.

title: Polarization and the real-spectrum specialization
notes: The multilinear \(V(\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_n)\) is described through the single-polytope functional; it is ordinary mixed volume when all spectra are real. In one variable a perimeter appears.
statement: There is a symmetric Minkowski-multilinear polarization \(P_n(\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_n)\) whose diagonal is the preceding face functional. For bodies in the same real form \(\mathbb R^n\subset\mathbb C^n\), it is ordinary mixed volume in the normalization \(V(K,\ldots,K)=\operatorname{Vol}_n(K)\). For \(n=1\), \(P_1\) is half the planar perimeter, with a line segment assigned perimeter twice its length. Thus the one-variable leading zero count is \(\operatorname{Perimeter}(\Gamma)R/(2\pi)\).
reconstruction: The polarization and semiperimeter normalization explain the unspecified constant in the notes. The statement is not ordinary \(2n\)-dimensional mixed volume of complex polytopes.
fate: The exact polarization is \citet[Propositions 1--2 and opening comparison, pp.347--348]{kazarnovskii1981zeros}. The paper appeared in 1981 and records receipt on 6 November 1980; receipt is not treated as evidence of public circulation. The seminar report on 23 February 1981 is the verified oral occurrence.
present_status: As of November 2026, the mixed pseudovolume and real-spectrum reduction are established.

title: Smooth-boundary and Levi-form descriptions of pseudovolume
notes: The notes extend the polytope functional to bodies with smooth boundary, introduce the complex tangent hyperplane, symmetrize the second fundamental form, and write an integral of the product of Levi eigenvalues, labelled \(S(\Delta)\).
statement: For a bounded domain \(K\subset\mathbb C^n\) with smooth boundary, let \(\nu\) be its outward unit normal and \(\alpha(v)=\langle v,i\nu\rangle\) on \(\partial K\). The normalized extension is \[P_n(K)=\frac1{\kappa_n n!}\int_{\partial K}\alpha\wedge(d\alpha)^{n-1}.\] For convex bodies it agrees with the polytope functional by approximation. On the complex tangent space \(H=T\partial K\cap iT\partial K\), the Hermitian part of the second fundamental form is the Levi form; the integral can equivalently be expressed through its determinant with the convention-dependent numerical factor.
reconstruction: The notebook's final label conflates the dimensionless face-angle factor \(S(\Delta)\) with the integrated body functional. Its division by two in defining the Hermitian part changes the Levi eigenvalue normalization, so no unverified factor is attached to its eigenvalue-product formula. The contact-form expression fixes a consistent normalization independently.
fate: All three constructions are read in \citet[\S1(a)--(c), p.348]{kazarnovskii1981zeros}; the paper explicitly allows nonconvex smooth domains for the first two boundary expressions. The paper appeared in 1981 and records receipt on 6 November 1980; receipt is not treated as evidence of public circulation. The seminar report on 23 February 1981 is the verified oral occurrence.
present_status: As of November 2026, the normalized boundary construction is established; the notebook's notation and unsupplied eigenvalue factor require qualification.

title: Support functions and the growth-indicatrix question of 2 March
notes: P000963 ends by mentioning a support-function formulation. On 2 March 1981, I. M. Gelfand asks on P000964 to relate Kazarnovskii's result to the growth indicatrix.
statement: With \(d^c=i(\bar\partial-\partial)\) and \(h_j=h_{\Gamma_j}\), the precise bridge is \[P_n(\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_n)=\frac1{\kappa_n n!}\int_{B_1}dd^ch_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dd^ch_n.\] These positive currents are well defined for the continuous convex support functions, by smooth approximation. For a finite exponential sum, \(\log|f(tz)|/t\leq h_\Gamma(z)+O(1/t)\); if one spectral exponent uniquely maximizes the real pairing at a direction, the limit equals the support function at that direction. Exceptional directions require the usual upper regularization of the indicator. Poincaré--Lelong converts logarithmic growth to zero currents. Passing to a product of zero currents or to a fixed-system remainder still requires appropriate regularity; individual pointwise bounds alone do not justify that passage.
reconstruction: The statement answers the requested structural relation without turning it into an unrestricted convergence conjecture. The date and intervening speaker are explicit. The support-function integral already occurs in the 1981 publication, so the connection is not credited solely to much later work.
fate: \citet[\S1(c), p.348]{kazarnovskii1981zeros} gives the exact support-function expression. \citet[Definition 5 and Theorems 1--2]{kazarnovskii2024distribution} later treats averaged zero currents for finite-dimensional spaces whose normalized evaluation norms converge locally uniformly to the support function; that is a precise extension with averaging, published 11 July 2024 after submissions in 2023 and 2024. Its displayed HTML normalizations are not imported here. The factor above uses the 1981 real-volume normalization and is checked on an interval.
present_status: As of November 2026, the finite-spectrum support-function connection is established, and later averaged generalizations have precise regularity assumptions. The notebook sentence supplies no broader independently stated open conjecture.
